name: Sugar diet (Peat-style fruit and sugar)

card.summary: A fruit-and-sugar-heavy eating pattern, drawn from Ray Peat's ideas, that looksmaxxing users adopt hoping for a leaner build, clearer skin and a push to IGF-1 and facial bone mass.
card.note: Reviews of high added-sugar intake link it to metabolic and cardiovascular problems; no trial has tested the diet for appearance outcomes.

quick.overview:
The sugar diet is an eating style in which a large share of daily calories comes from fruit, juice, honey and refined sugar, usually with low fat and some dairy or gelatin. In looksmaxxing circles it descends from the writings of Ray Peat and is promoted for leanness, skin and, in the more ambitious claims, growth of facial bone mass.

Proponents argue that sugar raises insulin and IGF-1, which they connect to bone and soft-tissue growth, and that fruit-based eating keeps people lean and their skin clear. Other forum users dispute the bone claim. No published trial has tested the diet for appearance, and nutrition research on high added-sugar intake focuses on metabolic health.
quick.how: Followers describe building meals around fruit, orange juice, honey, white sugar and sometimes milk, with large daily sugar targets quoted in forum threads. Some blend sugar into drinks. Threads describe it as a lifestyle rather than a short course, and say it is often paired with lifting and with limiting fat.
quick.risks: Reviews of diets high in added sugar associate them with metabolic, cardiovascular and mood-related problems, and forum users themselves describe very large daily sugar amounts as harmful. People with diabetes or blood-sugar conditions are generally advised by clinicians to limit added sugar. The diet is not regulated or standardized, and quantities quoted online vary widely.

lead: The sugar diet, often called the Peat-style diet or the frutarian diet in looksmaxxing forums, is an eating pattern built around fruit, fruit juice, honey and refined sugar. It descends from the writings of biologist Ray Peat (1936-2022), whose ideas about carbohydrate and metabolism circulate in bodybuilding and wellness communities, and has been adopted on looksmax.org by users who want to look leaner, have clearer skin and, in some posts, increase facial bone mass.[1][2][7][9]

The appearance chain proponents describe runs through hormones and metabolism: abundant sugar is said to keep metabolic rate and thyroid function high and to raise insulin and IGF-1, which is then linked to leanness, skin condition, and bone and tissue growth. Participants in the threads disagree about whether the growth claim holds, with some calling it unfounded and others recommending that readers try it themselves.[2][3][7]

No published clinical trial has tested a Peat-style fruit-and-sugar diet for appearance outcomes. Published research examines high-sugar diets in general, mostly in terms of metabolic, cardiovascular and oral health, and the World Health Organization recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of energy intake.[4][5]

chain: Fruit, juice and sugar make up most of the calories
Believers say insulin and IGF-1 rise and metabolism speeds up
Claimed result: a leaner body, clearer skin and more facial bone mass
angle.text: Followers eat large amounts of fruit and sugar in the belief that it supports a lean physique and drives growth signalling such as IGF-1 that they tie to facial bone development. Reports on looksmax.org are anecdotal, and members dispute the bone-growth part.

infobox: Fruit, juice, honey, refined sugar; often milk or gelatin [7]
WHO: free sugars under 10% of energy intake [5]
None on this diet for appearance

paras: The sugar diet makes simple carbohydrate the centre of daily eating. Fruit and juice are the staples, supplemented in many accounts by white sugar or honey, with moderate protein from dairy or gelatin and relatively little fat. Forum posts give a wide range of sugar targets, up to several hundred grams a day, and some users describe blending white sugar into a drink.[2][6]

It overlaps with the broader Ray Peat diet but is discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a distinct tactic, usually with the specific aim of changing physique, skin or facial bone mass instead of general wellness. Several thread titles frame it as a question, such as whether it works or whether it is the only way to stay lean naturally.[1][6]

According to the biography on his website, Peat held a PhD in biology from the University of Oregon with a specialty in physiology, began research on progesterone and related hormones in 1968, and published papers in 1971 and 1972 in Physiological Chemistry and Physics. He taught at several institutions and offered private nutritional counselling.[8] He died on 24 November 2022 aged 86, and an obituary on the IM-1776 site described his work as a broad, philosophical science that is often reduced to simplified diets and protocols.[9]

Peat's essay on sugar argues that sugar, and fructose in particular, is misunderstood: he writes that it is protective rather than the cause of diabetes and obesity, that sucrose and fructose are less fattening than starch or glucose, and that polyunsaturated seed oils are the more important problem. He ties a high metabolic rate to thyroid function, argues that stress hormones suppress sugar metabolism, and recommends milk, orange juice, fruit and honey, describing refined sugar as an occasional option when good fruit or honey is unavailable.[7] He also argues that research favourable to sugar is ignored or framed negatively by the medical profession.[7]

The looksmaxxing version is narrower than Peat's essays. It keeps the idea of sugar as a metabolic fuel but adds claims about IGF-1 and bone growth that, in the threads reviewed, are attributed to content creators rather than to Peat himself.[2]

A thread started by a user who had heard the idea from a looksmaxxing content creator asks whether roughly 500 g of sugar a day increases bone mass, and one reply says the poster drinks blended sugar twice a day and advises trying it personally.[2] Another thread asks whether the diet is a ploy to remove competition or whether the IGF-1 claim is real; replies mention insulin spikes, acne and heavy intake targets.[1]

Critics in the same community argue that liver IGF-1 matters less for bone growth than locally produced IGF-1 in cartilage cells, that a sugar-driven spike would be short-lived, and that sustained intake would risk insulin resistance and fat gain.[3] Another reply to the bone-mass thread doubted that the mandible and chin could change as much as claimed and said that half a kilo of sugar is harmful by any standard.[2] A separate thread asks whether a high-sugar diet is the only way to stay lean naturally.[6]

Narrative reviews of high-sugar diets describe added sugar in processed food as associated with metabolic, cardiovascular and nervous system disorders and with changes in reward signalling and mood.[4] A 2026 umbrella review of systematic reviews on free sugar found consistent links with 18 adverse outcomes, strongest for type 2 diabetes, obesity, cardiovascular and all-cause mortality and oral disease; most included studies looked at sugar-sweetened drinks, and most reviews were of low or critically low methodological quality.[10]

The WHO's 2015 guideline recommends keeping free sugars below 10 percent of energy intake, with a conditional recommendation for below 5 percent (about 25 g a day) for added benefit. It excludes sugars naturally present in fresh fruit, vegetables and milk, and cites associations between sugar intake and weight and dental caries.[5] Peat's essay takes the opposite position on sugar and obesity, and proponents say mainstream research reflects institutional bias.[7]

Skin is a stated goal of the diet. Recent narrative reviews describe biologically plausible links between glycemic instability and skin dysfunction, and between ultra-processed, insulin-raising diets and acne through insulin and mTOR signalling, while noting that direct evidence is limited and that further research is needed.[11][12] These reviews concern glycemic and ultra-processed diets generally, not fruit-based eating.

No published study found has tested whether a high-sugar diet changes facial bone mass in adults. The IGF-1 mechanism is discussed on looksmax.org, where one user argues it depends on locally produced IGF-1 in growth-plate cartilage rather than on liver output.[3]

Reviews link diets high in added sugar to obesity, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular outcomes and dental disease.[5][10] Forum users themselves describe very large daily sugar amounts as harmful, and one reply to a bone-mass thread jokes that heavy intake leads to acne.[1][2] People with diabetes or blood-sugar conditions are generally advised by clinicians to limit added sugar. The pattern described by proponents differs from the sugars the WHO excludes from its limit, since fruit, vegetables and milk are not counted, while refined sugar and juice are.[5]

No studies found. No published trial has tested a Peat-style fruit-and-sugar diet for leanness, skin appearance or facial bone changes. Related literature covers high-added-sugar diets in general and their metabolic and cardiovascular associations,[4][10] and trials of reducing free sugars for other outcomes, such as an 8-week open-label randomized trial of a low free sugar diet in adolescent boys with fatty liver disease.[13]

timeline.event: Ray Peat begins research on progesterone and related hormones, per his website biography.[8]
Peat completes his dissertation and publishes in Physiological Chemistry and Physics (papers in 1971 and 1972).[8]
The WHO issues a guideline recommending free sugars stay below 10 percent of energy intake.[5]
A randomized trial of a low free sugar diet in adolescent boys with fatty liver disease is published in JAMA.[13]
Peat dies on 24 November; a narrative review of high-sugar diets and health is published in Nutrients the same year.[9][4]
An umbrella review links free sugar intake to 18 adverse health outcomes.[10]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org the sugar diet appears in recurring threads that ask whether it works, mostly following claims by content creators about bone mass.[1][2]

claims.claim: Eating hundreds of grams of sugar a day raises IGF-1 and increases facial bone mass
claims.believers: Users who follow the idea say sugar elevates insulin and IGF-1, which they link to bone growth, and cite a creator's physique change as an example.[2]
claims.experts: No published study has measured facial bone change from a high-sugar diet. Forum critics argue that locally produced IGF-1 in cartilage drives bone growth rather than liver IGF-1.[3]

claims.claim: A fruit-and-sugar diet keeps people lean
claims.believers: Posters ask whether a high-sugar approach is the main way to stay lean naturally; Peat's essay argues sucrose and fructose are less fattening than starch and raise energy expenditure.[6][7]
claims.experts: The WHO cites an association between higher sugar intake and weight gain, and no trial has tested this diet for body composition.[5]

claims.claim: Sugar is not the cause of obesity or diabetes; stress and seed oils are
claims.believers: Peat argues that these conditions reflect impaired sugar metabolism and that mainstream research is skewed.[7]
claims.experts: An umbrella review of systematic reviews found consistent links between free sugar and type 2 diabetes and obesity, while noting low methodological quality in most included reviews.[10]

claims.claim: A sugar-rich diet clears or improves skin
claims.believers: Followers expect a high metabolic rate and balanced hormones to show up in skin quality.[1][7]
claims.experts: Reviews link glycemic instability and insulin-raising diets to skin problems such as acne through plausible mechanisms and say direct evidence is limited.[11][12]

claims.claim: Refined sugar is a poor substitute for fruit or honey
claims.believers: Peat describes refined sugar as an occasional option and prefers fruit, juice and honey; some looksmaxxing posters instead drink blended white sugar.[2][7]
claims.experts: The WHO's limit counts free sugars including juice and honey but excludes sugars in intact fresh fruit.[5]

claims.claim: Very large sugar intakes are harmful regardless of aim
claims.believers: Some forum members state that half a kilo of sugar a day is harmful by any standard and that heavy intake would risk insulin resistance.[2][3]
claims.experts: Reviews link high added-sugar diets with cardiometabolic risk factors such as obesity and type 2 diabetes.[4][10]
